_note: Evergreen facts. Keep them conservative and verifiable; add a 'source' note for your own records when you extend this list.

facts.headline: The first chairlift was installed at Sun Valley, Idaho, in 1936.
facts.detail: Engineers reportedly adapted a system used to load bananas onto ships. Sun Valley had opened as a purpose-built ski resort that same year.

facts.headline: Snowmaking depends on wet-bulb temperature, not just air temperature.
facts.detail: Dry air lets water droplets cool as they evaporate, so snow guns can make snow at higher air temperatures when humidity is low.

facts.headline: Snow guns come in two main types: fan guns and snow lances.
facts.detail: Fan guns blow atomised water through cold air with a large fan. Lances are tall poles that spray water and compressed air from height.

facts.headline: One cubic metre of water makes roughly two cubic metres of machine-made snow.
facts.detail: The exact ratio varies with temperature, humidity and equipment, but a rule of thumb of about 1:2 is widely used in the industry.

facts.headline: Detachable chairlifts slow down in the station, then speed up on the line.
facts.detail: Chairs release from the moving haul rope so skiers can board slowly while the lift still carries more people per hour than a fixed-grip chairlift.

facts.headline: Southern Hemisphere ski seasons run roughly from June to October.
facts.detail: Resorts in Chile, Argentina, Australia and New Zealand operate while the Alps and Rockies are in summer.

facts.headline: Japan's heavy powder comes from cold air crossing the Sea of Japan.
facts.detail: Cold winter winds from the Asian continent pick up moisture over the relatively warmer sea and drop it as snow on the mountains.

facts.headline: The Three Valleys in France is commonly cited as the world's largest linked ski area.
facts.detail: Figures of around 600 km of marked pistes are often quoted for the connected area.

facts.headline: Piste difficulty colours differ between Europe and North America.
facts.detail: In Europe pistes are typically graded blue, red and black. In North America trails use green circles, blue squares and black diamonds.

facts.headline: Fresh powder snow is mostly air.
facts.detail: Newly fallen snow is a loose mix of ice crystals and trapped air, which is why it is so much lighter than packed or machine-made snow.

facts.headline: Ski patrols trigger controlled avalanches before slopes open.
facts.detail: Trained teams use explosives or other methods to release unstable snow on purpose, making terrain safer for skiers.

facts.headline: Snowcats groom pistes overnight so the surface can set.
facts.detail: Grooming machines till, level and compact the snow. As it settles and refreezes, the surface becomes firmer by morning.
